--- title: "A Grammar of Graphics" filters: - quarto - line-highlight --- ::: {.cell} ::: ## TWO MINUTE CHALLENGE 🔮 👽 👼 {.inverse} Write down as many types of data plots that you can think of. ::: columns ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: ::: {.column width="70%"} [Go to menti.com and enter code 2979 2396](https://www.menti.com/al44t5ak5nwj) 🕐 `You've got 2 minutes!`{=html} ::: ::: ##
## What is a data plot? {.smaller} - data - **aesthetics: mapping of variables to graphical elements** - geom: type of plot structure to use - transformations: log scale, ... - layers: multiple geoms, multiple data sets, annotation - facets: show subsets in different plots - themes: modifying style ## Why? - With the grammar, a data plot becomes a **statistic**. - It is a functional mapping from variable to graphical element. Then we can do statistics on charts! - With a grammar, we don't have individual animals in the zoo, we have the genetic code that says how one plot is related to another plot. ## Elements of the grammar ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ``` ggplot(data = ) + ( mapping = aes(), stat = , position = ) + + ``` ::: ::: {.column .tightlist width="50%"} 7 key elements: - **DATA** - **GEOM_FUNCTION** - **MAPPINGS** - STAT - POSITION - COORDINATE_FUNCTION - FACET_FUNCTION ::: ::: ## Example: Tuberculosis data (Current) TB case notifications data from [WHO](http://www.who.int/tb/country/data/download/en/). Also available via R package [`getTBinR`](https://github.com/seabbs/getTBinR). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(tb_us, aes(x = year, y = count, fill = sex)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") + facet_grid(~ age) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/make-a-barchart-of-US-TB-incidence-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## **TWO MINUTE CHALLENGE** 🔮 👽 👼 {.inverse} Go to menti.com and enter code 2979 2396 - What do you learn about tuberculosis incidences in the USA from this plot? - Give three changes to the plot that would improve it. ## Results 🔮 👽 👼
::: notes - Incidence is declining, in all age groups, except possibly 15-24 - Much higher incidence for over 65s and 35-44 year olds - We do not know the underlying population size - There appears to be a structural change around 2008. Either a recording change or a policy change? - Missing information for 1998 # no longer true - Cannot compare counts for male/female using stacked bars, maybe fill to 100% to focus on proportion - Colour scheme is not color blind proof, switch to better palette - Axis labels, and tick marks? ::: ## Fix the plot Manually selected fill colors; theme with white background for better contrast ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="5,6"} # This uses a color blind friendly scale ggplot(tb_us, aes(x=year, y=count, fill=sex)) + geom_bar(stat="identity") + facet_grid(~age_group) + scale_fill_manual("Sex", values = c("#DC3220", "#005AB5")) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/colour-and-axes-fixes-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: [[Color deficiency friendly color schemes](https://davidmathlogic.com/colorblind/#%23005AB5-%23DC3220)]{.bottom} ## Compare males and females ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="3,4"} ggplot(tb_us, aes(x=year, y=count, fill=sex)) + geom_bar(stat="identity", position="fill") + ylab("proportion") + facet_grid(~age_group) + scale_fill_manual("Sex", values = c("#DC3220", "#005AB5")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/compare-proportions-of-males-females-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## 🔮 👽 👼 **TWO MINUTE CHALLENGE** {.inverse} - What do we learn about the data that is different from the previous plot? - What is easier and what is harder or impossible to learn from this arrangement? ::: notes - Focus is now on proportions of male and female each year, within age group - Proportions are similar across year - Roughly equal proportions at young and old age groups, more male incidence in middle years ::: ## Separate plots ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="5"} # Make separate plots for males and females, focus on counts by category ggplot(tb_us, aes(x=year, y=count, fill=sex)) + geom_bar(stat="identity") + scale_fill_manual("Sex", values = c("#DC3220", "#005AB5")) + facet_grid(sex~age_group) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/compare-counts-of-males-females-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: notes - Counts are generally higher for males than females - There are very few female cases in the middle years - Perhaps something of a older male outbreak in 2007-8, and possibly a young female outbreak in the same years ::: ## Make a pie ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="6"} # How to make a pie instead of a barchart - not straight forward ggplot(tb_us, aes(x=year, y=count, fill=sex)) + geom_bar(stat="identity") + facet_grid(sex~age_group) + scale_fill_manual("Sex", values = c("#DC3220", "#005AB5")) + coord_polar() + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/rose-plot-of-males-females-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: This isn't a pie, it's a [rose plot](https://datavizcatalogue.com/methods/nightingale_rose_chart.html)! ## Stacked bar ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="3"} # Step 1 to make the pie ggplot(tb_us, aes(x = 1, y = count, fill = factor(year))) + geom_bar(stat="identity", position="fill") + facet_grid(sex~age_group) + scale_fill_viridis_d("", option="inferno") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/stacked-barchart-of-males-females-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: ## Pie chart ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="3,4,7"} # Now we have a pie, note the mapping of variables # and the modification to the coord_polar ggplot(tb_us, aes(x = 1, y = count, fill = factor(year))) + geom_bar(stat="identity", position="fill") + facet_grid(sex~age_group) + scale_fill_viridis_d("", option="inferno") + coord_polar(theta = "y") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/pie-chart-of-males-females-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## 🔮 👽 👼 **TWO MINUTE CHALLENGE** {.inverse} - What are the pros, and cons, of using the pie chart for this data? - Would it be better if the pies used age for the segments, and facetted by year (and sex)? Go to menti.com and enter code 2979 2396 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ## Line plot vs barchart ::: {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(tb_us, aes(x=year, y=count, colour=sex)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + facet_grid(~age_group) + scale_colour_manual("Sex", values = c("#DC3220", "#005AB5")) + ylim(c(0,NA)) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/use a line plot instead of bar-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.smaller} - We can read counts for both sexes - Males and females can be directly compared - Temporal trend is visible ::: ## Line plot vs barchart ::: {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tb_us |> group_by(year, age_group) |> summarise(p = count[sex=="m"]/sum(count)) |> ggplot(aes(x=year, y=p)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.50, colour="grey50", linewidth=2) + geom_line() + geom_point() + facet_grid(~age_group) + ylab("Proportion of Males") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/use a line plot of proportions-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ::: ::: tightlist ::: {.smaller} - Attention is forced to proportion of males - Direct comparison of counts within year and age - Equal proportion guideline provides a baseline for comparison ::: ::: ## Your turn {.inverse .middle} Make sure you can make all the TB plots just shown. If you have extra time, try to: - Facet by gender, and make line plots of counts of age. - Show the points only, and overlay a linear model fit. ::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} ``{=html} ::: ## Resources {.smaller} - [posit cheatsheets](https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/) - [ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis, Hadley Wickham](https://ggplot2-book.org) - [ggplot2 web site](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org) - [R Graphics Cookbook, Winston Chang](http://www.cookbook-r.com/Graphs/) - [Data Visualization, Kieran Healy](https://socviz.co) - [Data Visualization with R, Rob Kabacoff](https://rkabacoff.github.io/datavis/index.html) - [Fundamentals of Data Visualization, Claus O. Wilke](https://serialmentor.com/dataviz/) ::: bottom This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
